notes:
I've completed notes for all eight verses. Each point gives its source page. Some things I couldn't find with the searches I had:
- No Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter (I only found how Catholic Bible translations render it).
- No Protestant traditions really disagreeing.
- Nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching.

Those gaps are left blank as you asked.

---

**v. 1 – Joab at Rabbah; David stays home**
- **Why spring?** Wars usually weren't fought in winter because rain and cold made travel and campaigning hard, so fighting started again in spring.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/
- **A note on the Hebrew word "kings":** The standard Hebrew text in 2 Samuel 11:1 has a similar-looking word, "messengers." Here Chronicles has the right word, "kings."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-1.htm
- **The missing story:** Guzik says David should have been at the battle. What happened while he stayed in Jerusalem (adultery with Bathsheba, then plotting Uriah's murder with Joab) was so well known that the Chronicler didn't need to tell it.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/
- **Matthew Henry:** "David tarried at Jerusalem" is only a hint of the sin. Had David been with the army he would have avoided that temptation. Henry also says that leaving the sin out teaches us not to enjoy repeating other people's faults.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_020.cfm
- **Adam Clarke:** The Chronicler skips the Bathsheba story, as he deliberately skips almost everything that would hurt David's reputation.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-chronicles-20.html
- **Utley (quoted on Precept Austin):** Leaving it out fits the Chronicler's aim of honouring David and his royal line.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
- **Wiersbe (quoted on Precept Austin):** Sin begins when we neglect our duty. David was in more danger in Jerusalem than on the battlefield. Precept Austin also quotes Walton: Assyrian and Babylonian records often say campaigns began in March–May. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
- **David restored:** Guzik notes from 2 Samuel 12:26–31 that Joab called David in to finish the conquest after his repentance. This was the last step of David's restoration, and his sin didn't doom him to a life of failure.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/

**v. 2 – The crown**
- **Guzik:** David's sin didn't cost him his crown, because he answered Nathan with confession and repentance.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/
- **Selman (quoted by Guzik):** Ammon seems to have been reduced to the status of a province.  Guzik adds that the plunder was taken back to Jerusalem for the future temple.  Same URL.
- **Weight:** About 75 lbs (34 kg).  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
- **"Their king" or the god Milcom? Commentators disagree:**
  - Ellicott reads it as "Milcom" or "Moloch," the Ammonite god. He says a crown that heavy would suit a big idol's head better than a man's.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-20.html
  - Konkel (quoted on Precept Austin) agrees it should be read as Milcom.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
  - The NET Bible note disagrees. It says part of the Greek tradition was wrong to read "their king" as the name Milcom.  Same URL.
- **How could anyone wear it?** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) think it was hung above the throne on gold chains rather than worn.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/1-chronicles-20.html Ellicott offers two options: David made a crown out of it (the Latin Vulgate's reading), or attendants held it over his head.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-20.html
- **Pulpit Commentary (application):** The crown of God's favour and of righteousness is far better than this one.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-20.html

**v. 3 – Forced labour or torture? (the main debate in this chapter)**
- **Forced labour (the majority view):**
  - Precept Austin says most commentaries and translations read this as David making the Ammonites his labourers, though some think he killed them.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
  - Cambridge Bible: the tools suggest hard labour, not a massacre.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-3.htm
  - JFB: the Hebrew word differs by one letter from "put them" in 2 Samuel 12:31, and many take it to mean hard penal servitude.  Same URL.
  - Pulpit Commentary: the verb is uncertain. It may mean hard work farming and making bricks. Saws and harrows would also be odd torture tools when ordinary weapons were close at hand.  Same URL.
  - BibleHub's study notes: the tools are for cutting wood and dressing stone, materials later stockpiled for the temple.  https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/20-3.htm
- **Torture (the other side):**
  - Keil & Delitzsch say both accounts describe the prisoners being killed "in the cruellest way."  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-3.htm
  - Ellicott doesn't try to excuse it: by the standards of that age it was "a glorious revenge."  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-chronicles-20.html
  - MacArthur allows both readings. On the torture reading, David treated the captives the way Ammonites treated others.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
  - Omanson's note (on Precept Austin) says the Hebrew text as it stands most likely means torture.  Same URL.
- **A middle view:** Even the Pulpit Commentary's homily section regrets David's cruelty, while saying he shouldn't be judged by modern standards.  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-chronicles-20.html
- **Catholic translations (not commentary):** The Douay-Rheims renders the verse as the people being "cut and bruised to pieces," while the modern Catholic New American Bible has them "set... to work."  https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/20-3.htm
- **Does this show the Chronicler protecting David?** Keil says no. The Chronicler skips the harsh treatment of Moab but still records this, so whitewashing can't be his reason.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-1.htm
- **What's skipped before v. 4:** The Chronicler leaves out Absalom's and Sheba's rebellions and the Gibeonite revenge on Saul's family (2 Samuel 13:1–21:14).  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-3.htm

**v. 4 – Sibbecai kills Sippai**
- **Guzik:** These victories show Israel could kill giants without David, and that God raises up new leaders as the old ones leave the scene.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/
- **Matthew Henry:** The giants of Gath were the last Philistines to fall, just as the sons of Anak were last in Joshua's day. Some sins are like these giants and are only beaten after a long struggle.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_020.cfm
- **Clarke (quoted by Guzik):** Amnon's incest and Absalom's rebellion belong before this verse. The Chronicler left them out because they were already well recorded.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/

**v. 5 – Elhanan and Lahmi**
- **Traditional view:**
  - GotQuestions: this verse settles the question raised by 2 Samuel 21:19. A scribe probably miscopied "the brother of" there, so David killed Goliath and Elhanan later killed his brother.  https://www.gotquestions.org/Goliath-David-Elhanan.html
  - NET Bible note: the Samuel text misread the Hebrew word for "brother" as a grammatical marker. The original probably read "killed the brother of Goliath."  https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=2Sa+21:19+21:20
  - Coffman offers another option: there may simply have been more than one giant called Goliath.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/17-3.html
- **Modern critical view:** The ISBE article on the NET Bible site says most modern critics think the Chronicler changed his source to make it agree with 1 Samuel 17.  https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Elhanan
- **The spear "like a weaver's beam":** Selman (quoted by Guzik) says it was a javelin with a loop and cord for range and stability, known in the Aegean from the 1100s BC.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/

**v. 6 – The giant with six fingers and toes**
- **Rapha / Rephaim:** Selman (quoted by Guzik) says the Rephaim were an ancient people of Canaan, famous for their size.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/ Precept Austin notes "Rapha" may be a family name.  https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-20-commentary
- **Literal or symbolic?** BibleHub's Q&A page says some read the extra digits figuratively, but there's no strong reason to reject the literal reading.  https://biblehub.com/q/1_chronicles_20_6__is_the_giant's_anatomy_real.htm
- **Text notes:** Cambridge Bible says the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 21:20 calls him "a man of contention," meaning a challenger or champion.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-6.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** An extra finger or toe is nothing against the Almighty.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_020.cfm

**v. 7 – Jonathan kills the giant who taunted Israel**
- **Matthew Henry:** The giants defied Israel and paid for it. Those who mock God and his people are the most plainly marked for ruin.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ch/1Ch_020.cfm
- **Guzik:** David's legacy was the people he trained for victory.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/

**v. 8 – "By the hands of David and his servants"**
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** This doesn't mean David killed any of them himself. "By the hand of" can mean "through," so the giants fell in David's wars, by his servants.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/20-1.htm
- **Guzik:** Since Goliath came from Gath, these were his sons or brothers.  David's wins now would make things better for Solomon later.  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-20/
- **Pointing to Christ (Henry, with Benson the Methodist commentator saying the same):** Henry says the Son of David's victories, like David's, come step by step. Death, the last enemy, will be beaten like these giants.   https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/20-6.html
